items.body: @avagin @ayushr2 let me know if you'd prefer this in separate PRs.
@nixprime could you take a loot at this pr too?
@avagin could you import this so that tests run? I haven't run all the tests yet (still need #12461).

@tamird Have we benchmarked the new ilist or refs implementation compared to their old go_generics one? IIRC, with Go generics, we add interface method calls and these types are on the hot paths for various subsystems.
Thanks very much for the analysis! That makes sense, at least for ilist. How about the second commit that touches refs?

I think the refs case is fine, with some changes:

- The `LoggingPolicy` type argument has the same same-shape problem, resulting in an indirect call to `LoggingPolicy.enabled()` in every `IncRef/TryIncRef/DecRef`:

- An ergonomic complaint: having to explicitly specify `refs.LoggingDisabled` everywhere is a bit obnoxious, since the intended use of the feature is that it's disabled by default, and selectively enabled to debug refcounting problems for specific types. Is it possible to define e.g. `type RefsBase[T any, L LoggingPolicy] struct{...}; type Refs[T any] = RefsBase[T, LoggingDisabled]; type LoggedRefs[T any] = RefsBase[T, LoggingEnabled]`?
Done. Required some more go_stateify surgery, please have a look!
Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

> Is there any benefits of using Go generics?

There's a big ergonomics benefit. Using bazel in editors is not very well supported, so anyone working on gvisor without the benefit of internal tooling can't easily jump to definition on types generated by `go_generics`.

It looks like it doesn't work in `bpf/input_bytes.go` anymore either... From experimentation, it looks like it works if `bpf.load*()` is inlined into a call site where `endian` is specified explicitly, but when it's inlined into e.g. `bpf.Exec[endian Endianness]()` the type-switch occurs at runtime. I'm asking the Go team if there's anything we can do about this.

Apparently this is https://github.com/golang/go/issues/59591.

I tried inlining `LogRefs()` into `IncRef()` etc. (`var l L; if _, ok := any(l).(loggingEnabled); ok { ... }`), but this didn't help the generated code.

Unlike go_generics, native Go generics only instantiate distinct code for different argument "shapes"; see https://github.com/golang/proposal/blob/master/design/generics-implementation-gcshape.md. AFAIU, all pointers have the same shape, so all instances of `ilist.Entry[*T]` and `ilist.List[*T]` use the same generated code, necessitating dynamic dispatch for `ilist.Linker` method calls after this change.

prs.title: atomicptr: use atomic.Pointer
prs.head: 9e17fdee10b5d7cde68732dbe86e823fdb34fe48

items.body: @ayushr2 could you have a look at this one?

IIUC, we are using `go_generics` package to generate code which is using Go's native generics support. Two levels of generated code. So why not directly replace the `go_generics` atomic pointer with `atomic.Pointer`? Maybe I am missing something. Is there a benefit to doing it this way?

> 

I couldn't agree more, but stateify doesn't yet support generics. That requires the first N-1 commits in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470, so I was planning to send that after that PR (and this one) merge.
Having said that, I could move those commits to this PR, since there is some question about whether https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470 can be merged at all.

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.
> 
> We should probably add native support to stateify for `atomic.Pointer`; such that it should be able to detect `atomic.Pointer` usage and generate code using .Load() and .Store(). I don't know if the AST parser we use is capable to do this.

It's not that the AST parser isn't capable, it's that that state package fundamentally wants to register a `reflect.Type` under a unique name: https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/70f9a824dc761638488b988ebd33930569a83c65/pkg/state/types.go#L339

Since there's no `reflect.Type` associated with an uninstantiated generic, we'd need to do string matching on the type's name and its methods to discover that it is an `atomic.Pointer`.

> If not, we can add support for new `stateify` tags like:
> 
> ```
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state: pointer".(int)"`
> ```

We perhaps could, but is that any better? This would make a poor addition to `go_stateify` because it doesn't generalize beyond `atomic.Pointer`.

> 
> If you intend to cleanup `atomicptr` from go_generics, then we could also just use:
> 
> ```
> // +stateify savable
> type S struct {
> 	// descriptorTable holds descriptors.
> 	ptr atomic.Pointer[int] `state:".(int)"`
> }
> 
> func (s *S) savePtr() int {
> 	return s.ptr.Load()
> }
> 
> func (s *S) loadPtr(_ goContext.Context, ptr int) {
> 	s.ptr.Store(ptr)
> }
> ```

We could, but that feels quite manual, and ergonomically worse than what exists today.

Before the codegen deficiencies were pointed out in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/12470#pullrequestreview-3645103398 my goal was to remove type parameter support from go_generics, leaving only constants.

Now answering your first point:

> IIUC [80913f9](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/80913f9c71a1e72d7999f736377d8bf245f873a1) requires wrapping the atomic pointer fields with a struct and putting special `stateify` tags on them. I think that is also not a very clean interface.

Well, I don't disagree, but haven't come up with a cleaner way of supporting generics with stateify. I'm all ears for suggestions!

source.title: checklocks: guard the TCP segment queue
source.body:
The segment queue uses mu for its list and frozen state, but checklocks does not enforce that ownership. Guard both fields and enforce the existing caller-held lock requirement of emptyLocked.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce UDP receive-state ownership
source.body:
Packet delivery reads frozen under rcvMu, but freeze, thaw, and restore write it under mu. Use rcvMu for all accesses and group frozen with the receive state it controls.

Annotate the receive fields and reuse thaw after successful restore so checklocks enforces the same ownership during normal operation and save/restore.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard socket option state
source.body:
SocketOptions documents locking for its error queue and linger option, but checklocks does not enforce those contracts. Add field guards using the mutexes already held by their accessors and replace the redundant locking prose.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: fix fragmentation shutdown locking
source.body:
The post-Release check added in a4fb3b200fdc returns an error while still holding mu, so a later Process or Release blocks indefinitely. Unlock before returning and enforce the existing outer-state and release-helper lock contracts.

Document how marking a reassembler done excludes further processing and gives release exclusive cleanup ownership. Timeout callbacks run with the fragmentation mutex held and cannot reenter the owner.

Cover processing after release followed by another release, and make existing internal-state inspections follow the guarded contract.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard gonet connection state
source.body:
Guard deadline timers and cancellation channels with the deadline mutex, and check the caller-held contract on setDeadline. Guard the TCP read buffer with readMu while preserving the readMu-before-deadline-mutex lock order.

Construct deadline state as a fresh value so initialization is visible to checklocks. Timer callbacks retain their captured cancellation channel, preserving deadline reset behavior without copying a used mutex.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce hostinet lock and atomic rules
source.body:
Require the persistent-event mutex for mask updates and direct waiter-entry operations while allowing lock-free atomic mask reads. Require atomic access to shutdown and backlog state.

Guard the collection of listeners awaiting restore with its collection mutex, retaining detached-list processing after unlocking.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: enforce link endpoint ownership
source.body:
Enforce existing mutex ownership of TUN endpoint associations and lifecycle state, shared veth state, and the nested endpoint dispatcher. TUN flags remain immutable for an association; readers capture the association under the device mutex before accessing flags without it. Final release remains a file-lifetime boundary.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard netlink port allocation
source.body:
The port manager serializes allocation and release with mu, including access to each protocol map. Annotate the ports field so checklocks enforces the existing contract, replacing the protection comment.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: guard receive timestamps and TCP_INQ
source.body:
Make checklocks enforce readMu ownership of socket-level timestamp state and TCP_INQ. Require the same lock in timestamp updates and receive control-message helpers.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: synchronize plugin readiness
source.body:
Plugin readiness checks read and clear a cache that the notifier updates under its own mutex. Readers do not acquire that mutex, so consuming cached events races with notification updates and other readiness checks. The unsynchronized cache dates to 079c1a937be.

Make the cache atomic and consume requested IN/OUT bits with a snapshot CAS. Preserve unrelated events and the existing fallback when not all requested I/O events are cached. Avoid acquiring the notifier mutex in Readiness, since notification callbacks can re-enter it.

Add a concurrent-readiness regression using disjoint cached I/O bits, retaining error, hangup, and high bits without invoking the plugin C implementation. Annotate the atomic cache and notifier registration contracts, and document the external owner of the remaining event state.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: checklocks: fix proc network sysctl ownership
source.body:
Proc file descriptions share sysctl sources, so per-FD locks do not protect cached state. source.body:
Two TCP state paths use atomic storage without preserving its synchronization contract.

The send-buffer option callback atomically disables autotuning without the endpoint or send-queue mutex, but endpoint probes copy the flag with RacyLoad. The first commit uses atomic snapshot accesses, declares the flag and queue-lock contracts, and extends the endpoint-probe regression with a concurrent option callback. Readiness and shutdown also update connection-direction bits under different mutexes. The load-then-swap added in 89b6a474c62 can lose a concurrent send-closed or receive-closed update. source.title: checklocks: publish initialized TCP endpoint IDs
source.body:
TCP ICMP errors read endpoint addresses and ports without taking the endpoint mutex since 62b4c2f5173. An active connection previously published its selected ephemeral tuple before assigning it to the endpoint, so an incoming error could race with that assignment or report a zero local port.

Assign the selected port before registering the endpoint and restore the old ID if registration fails. Taking the endpoint mutex in the ICMP reader would deadlock synchronous loopback errors during writes.

Extend the existing connect-error test to deliver a matching ICMP error as soon as the endpoint is registered. Pause the handshake clock before SYN allocation so later synchronization cannot hide the publication race.

prs.title: Keep metric field lookup nosplit
prs.head: f5f0270289147db0614fd2eadc1ed15dcb652f81

items.body: @EtiennePerot could you please TAL as the author of the commits mentioned in the description? I discovered this while investigating failures in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/14502.
@konstantin-s-bogom mind having a look here?
@EtiennePerot could you please take a look? once this lands I will put up another PR to fix the gap in checkescape that admitted this use of maps under nosplit.

> For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

no, things are getting *slower*. the implementation is going from using maps to using open-coded binary search, but that is what's needed here to preserve `nosplit`.
Great, ty! Once this lands I'll send the checkescape fixes that catch the map use in nosplit.

Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
For posterity, in the commit message: we are going from 12 ns/op -> 6 ns/op?

The commit message now explicitly states that the original paired ARM64 measurement showed lookup slowing from about 6.7 ns/op with a map to 12.5 ns/op with binary search, to preserve nosplit behavior.

Field lookup tests pass normally and with the race detector; Nogo and formatting also pass. The full ARM64 metric suite still hits the duration-bucketer failure covered by #14359, which I reproduced on current master as well. All builds and tests ran in Docker.

Assisted-by: Codex

Thanks for finding this out. I still think we can do better here, especially for large-cardinality metrics (e.g. syscall counters). Will work on that on my own, but approving anyway here though this might race.
Any idea why 48?

48 comes from [79b38029d](https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/79b38029d), whose commit message reports that linear search was faster than both map and binary search through 48 values. Added that direct citation to the comment in 13e28b4f1. This preserves the existing cutoff; I haven't remeasured the crossover with the current toolchain.

Assisted-by: Codex

Hoisted `targetAddr` before the binary-search loop in 13e28b4f1.

Assisted-by: Codex

Changed in 13e28b4f1: allocate `valuesSorted` at its final length, fill it with the original declaration indices, and sort in place with `slices.SortFunc`. The uniqueness check now uses `map[string]struct{}`.

Assisted-by: Codex

Minor nit on this comment: `valueIndices` is local to `NewField` and does not escape `NewField`. What ensures `v` escapes to the heap is that `allowedValues` (and `valuesSorted`) are stored into the returned `Field` struct, which callers assign to package-level vars or long-lived metric objects. For small fields ($\le 48$), `valuesSorted` is not constructed and `valueIndices` is dropped, but `v` is still retained in `Field.values`.

Changed construction to retain the pointers in the preallocated sorted slice and updated the comment in 13e28b4f1. One subtlety: a map can remain local while pointer values stored in it escape; Go 1.26.3's [map0 test](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_map.go#L13-L22) demonstrates this. Indexed slice stores likewise make the pointees escape ([slice6](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.3/test/escape_slice.go#L62-L68)), preserving stable heap addresses here. Small fields only use pointer equality.

Assisted-by: Codex

Minor nit, but otherwise approved. Thanks for the patch!

Updated to match the compiler's [ASCII-space split](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/noder/noder.go#L334-L339) and [single terminal CR removal](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/2dc996f71/src/cmd/compile/internal/syntax/parser.go#L169-L181). A trailing tab or NBSP remains part of the directive name, so `TrimSpace` would accept directives the compiler does not recognize. The analyzer reads the original comment bytes because `go/parser` removes interior CRs. Concrete and generic fixtures cover these distinctions; their Nogo checks pass for AMD64 and ARM64.

prs.title: Allocate process_vm test buffers per case
prs.head: e0f75c3ea08d7b74e1c757e9034285142c551309

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

> Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

In response to [your review](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15061#pullrequestreview-5399663055):

The original run was OOM-killed while enumerating tests, before any syscall case ran. It used a 300 MB scheduling estimate; I don't have evidence of the worker's hard memory limit. There are five parameterized tests, and [GoogleTest retains a parameter copy for each](https://github.com/google/googletest/blob/52eb8108c/googletest/include/gtest/internal/gtest-param-util.h#L402-L410). With two 32 MiB strings per parameter, that is at least 320 MiB of payload for registration alone, plus temporary copies.

After this change, all 50 cases passed in native and each of the two systrap variants with the same worker estimate. The actual 32 MiB syscall buffers are unchanged. The noncopying comparison also avoids duplicating and concatenating those large buffers while a case runs.

[Original run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/980d63fa-55b9-49d3-81d5-46ff7ca7cedb) · [After-fix run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/a20482e5-86cd-4bce-aa3c-1906c0a66d4a)

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
Is this really necessary? How tightly constrained are such workers?

A couple of minor non-blocking thoughts:
- In the binary entrypoint filegroups (`runsc`, `shim`, etc.), consider `glob(["*.go"], exclude = ["*_test.go"])` just to future-proof against any unit tests added to those top-level packages getting accidentally bundled into the export archive.
- In `BUILD`, `$(execpath go.mod)` is passed both to `--go-mod` and in the positional args list. Harmless since it just populates `files["go.mod"]`, but `assemble` could also just implicitly write `files["go.mod"] = data` from the already-read `--go-mod` file.
LGTM

Propagate failures from source lint tools

e362ccc8a added a lint summary that continues after individual checks fail. Calling each check in a conditional disables Bash errexit inside its helpers, so unsuccessful formatters, file selection, or installation can fall through to a successful result. Empty output from a failed formatter can be reported as clean, and --fix ignores formatter failures.

Run each check in an unconditional shell that stops on failures, including inside command substitutions, then collect its status for the summary. Preserve captured formatter status and diagnostics. Exercise these failure boundaries and continued reporting through the public lint entrypoint.

cc1plus: all warnings being treated as errors

source.title: Recognize complete dependency license texts
source.body:
Replace phrase-based classification with complete license-text matching
to avoid combining independent notices. The old matcher combined Arrow's
BSD terms and OpenSSL's advertising clause into BSD-4-Clause [1].

Delegate text matching and identifier ownership to google/licensecheck
[2], configured with the complete LLVM exception [3]. References alone
do not establish a license grant. Keep the scanner's identifiers literal
so policy review sees the distinctions the detector can establish.

Regenerate the catalog for the new classifier dependency and the legacy
University of Illinois/NCSA grants in LLVM [3] and Kythe [4], previously
reported as MIT. Scope the corresponding policy exceptions to these two
dependencies and record their redistribution conditions, retaining the
existing source versions and archive hashes.

[1]: https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/e03105efc/go/LICENSE.txt
[2]: https://github.com/google/licensecheck/blob/16aaea366/scan.go
[3]: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/cb2f0d0a5/LICENSE.TXT
[4]: https://github.com/kythe/kythe/blob/a182743b6/LICENSE#L205-L251

Assisted-by: Codex

prs.title: Build plugins with the selected C toolchain
prs.head: 007e776dd0bd266a8af950058f34cefaf9bbc10c

items.body:
Rebased onto current master, @EtiennePerot.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.
/gemini review

## Code Review

This pull request replaces the implicit external source downloads of the TLDK/DPDK plugin stack with pinned Bazel inputs built via `rules_foreign_cc`. It introduces several patches to support musl libc compatibility, replaces glibc's backtrace with `libbacktrace`, and adds a test for stack unwinding. The review feedback highlights three key issues: a thread-safety race condition in `capture_stack` due to concurrent redirection of the global DPDK log stream, a potential out-of-bounds write in the backtrace patch's `trace_frame` callback, and a build compatibility issue in `toolchain.bzl` where standard environments might fail the strict compiler check.

This adapter is compiled only into `backtrace_test`. Its only caller is
`TestDumpStack`, which calls it twice serially; neither call starts DPDK
workers or runs in parallel. Production stack dumping does not use this
capture adapter. A mutex here would therefore add no protection needed by
the current callers, and would not serialize unrelated DPDK log writers.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

The bound follows from the pinned library's callback contract:
[`backtrace_simple` stops when the callback returns nonzero](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/backtrace.h#L125-L131),
and its [implementation stops unwinding immediately](https://github.com/ianlancetaylor/libbacktrace/blob/793921876/simple.c#L83-L86).
Each dump starts with size zero. The callback writes indices 0 through
255, then returns 1, so it cannot enter again with size 256. I'll keep the
existing bound without a redundant precheck.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The strict check `toolchain.compiler not in ["gcc", "clang"]` can fail on standard environments (such as Linux with Bazel's autoconfigured toolchain) where `toolchain.compiler` is set to `"compiler"`. Since DPDK's makefiles and `rules_foreign_cc` already handle compiler compatibility and detection, this strict check is unnecessary and can be safely removed to avoid breaking the build on standard setups.

```suggestion
    toolchain = find_cc_toolchain(ctx)
```

The pinned rules_cc detector [returns `gcc` or `clang` for those compilers;
`compiler` is its fallback](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_cc/blob/21e14308c/cc/private/toolchain/unix_cc_configure.bzl#L290-L295).
Here the compiler identifier also selects DPDK's configuration through
`RTE_TARGET = x86_64-native-linuxapp-$(C_COMPILER)`. Removing this check
would pass the unsupported `compiler` configuration to DPDK rather than
make that toolchain work. I'll retain the explicit GCC/Clang requirement.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

@EtiennePerot I reproduced this on Linux 6.1.0 by attaching a
pass-through cgroup getsockopt hook. Short calls then return EFAULT

source.body:
Return ENOENT for missing original destinations

Match Linux's SO_ORIGINAL_DST result when conntrack has no matching connection [1]. Both the uninitialized-table guard and an initialized conntrack lookup returned ENOTCONN. The guard and syscall expectation introduced in b3ff31d04 prevented a panic but used the wrong errno.

Return the existing ENOENT error from both lookup paths. Extend the NAT reaping test to verify the original destination while tracked and the missing-connection error after reaping. Correct the syscall expectation, close its socket through FileDescriptor, and remove the unrelated raw socket capability requirement from this TCP query.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_proto.c#L254-L307

source.title: Bound TUN and TAP interface MTUs
source.body:
Bound TUN and TAP interface MTUs

The rtnetlink MTU setter added in 6dd4ef415 accepted any uint32 value for TUN and TAP devices. This also let callers enlarge the MTU used by the allocation guard in f51097051. Linux instead requires a minimum of 68 and a maximum of 65535 minus the device's link header length, returning EINVAL outside that range [1][2].

Give TUN-created NICs these bounds and check them before changing the endpoint MTU. Preserve the bounds when moving the NIC to another stack. Zero-valued NIC options remain unrestricted, preserving the policies of other link endpoints.

Exercise both rtnetlink setters for TUN and TAP at the valid boundaries and immediately outside them, including a high-bit value. Check that rejected requests preserve the MTU and that NIC moves preserve the bounds. These are interface configuration limits; the oversized-write allocation contract is unchanged.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/drivers/net/tun.c#L1372
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/net/core/dev.c#L8637

The only public-tree reference I found to `IPV6_CHECKSUM_SETSOCKOPT_SHORT_EXCEPTION` is this test. It was introduced in b488df0a2 with a TODO referring to b/212585236. Is the variable set by an internal test configuration, and should removing it here be accompanied by cleanup there?

source.title: Preserve moved TUN devices across restore
source.body:
Preserve moved TUN devices across restore

The TUN save/restore support in 8bf3dc484 classified preserved NICs by
kind, but moving a NIC to another network namespace discarded that kind.
A moved TUN device was consequently removed during checkpoint. Its
restored close callback also retained the original stack and NIC ID,
rather than the destination chosen by the move.

Keep the kind when moving a NIC. Restore its close callback in the stack
that owns the preserved NIC, and remove the stale ownership fields from
the TUN endpoint. Extend the syscall coverage to move a TUN device
before checkpoint and verify its removal when the restored device is
closed.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex

source.title: Restore pending NDP jobs at their deadlines
source.body:
Restore pending NDP jobs at their deadlines

IPv6 endpoints preserved by 8bf3dc484 recreated NDP jobs without
scheduling them. Routes, on-link prefixes, and SLAAC addresses learned
from router advertisements could consequently outlive their deadlines
after restore, and temporary address regeneration stopped.

Save each Job instance with its monotonic deadline and completion state.
Rebind its lock and callback on restore and rearm pending instances.
Restore NDP jobs through this shared mechanism.

Make ManualClock save its current time without live timers. The NDP
regressions save and load the full stack, then advance the new clock to
observe expiry and regeneration.

Updated the cleanup to match 962441d4e more closely: restore effective CAP_NET_RAW and return the thread to the runtime on success; leave it locked for disposal only if restoration fails. source.title: Build BPF with declared LLVM tools and headers
source.body:
Build BPF with declared LLVM tools and headers

BPF genrules used PATH clang and /usr/include, so remote compilation
required worker packages and cross builds used the worker's headers.

Compile BPF programs with LLVM's declared execution-platform tools,
target Linux UAPI headers and libbpf's helper headers. Keep the BPF v1
instruction set explicitly because the selected LLVM defaults to v3 [1].
Align the module versions required by LLVM. The supplier requires Bazel
8.5 or newer for its extension metadata API [2]. Leave Coral registered
for C and C++.

Remove the builder's libbpf-dev requirement. Record libbpf using its
BSD-2-Clause alternative [3]; its upstream notice requires a maintained
audit entry because the canonical classifier does not recognize it.

[1]: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/85ac56026/llvm/lib/Target/BPF/BPFSubtarget.cpp#L75
[2]: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/0b3c45f46
[3]: https://github.com/libbpf/libbpf/blob/f5dcbae73/LICENSE

Assisted-by: Codex

What's the point of documenting this?

The purpose is to give contributors a baseline when syscall expectations
vary between Linux kernels. #15233 is an example: a test passed on newer
Linux but needed different handling on older kernels. The public pipeline
names the worker pools without identifying the kernels they exercise.

Agreed that the exact releases move. The table records dated observations
with links to the CI logs; it is not a minimum-supported-kernel policy. It
also distinguishes which jobs exercise native Linux versus gVisor. Would
kernel series plus a link to the authoritative worker configuration be a
more useful way to document that coverage?

prs.head: 9c1aeb0686a60878ecb92d6fe7694324dfabebbe

items.body:
I compared the existing pointer, map, and slice state benchmarks on both
sides of this change. None of the six encoding/decoding cases showed a
statistically significant timing difference in this run; their median
allocation counts and bytes per operation were unchanged.

I also benchmarked `tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` with a nonzero
`Timestamp`, so this measures the old UnixNano hook against the new binary
codec through a real caller:

| Operation | Before | After | Change | Allocs before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Save | 9.710 µs | 12.207 µs | +25.72% | 80 → 94 |
| Load | 12.674 µs | 13.997 µs | +10.44% | 138 → 151 |

Allocated bytes increased from 5,624 to 6,528 per save and from 6,024 to
6,320 per load. The encoded message grew from 494 to 521 bytes. The time
comparison was significant for save (p<0.001) and load (p=0.015), with ten
samples per version.

Both binaries were compiled first, then measured in ten alternating
before/after pairs on one Linux AMD EPYC worker, pinned to the same CPU
with GOMAXPROCS=1 and Go 1.27.1. Each benchmark used a 500 ms duration;
two warmups were excluded. These are state-serialization microbenchmarks,
not whole-sandbox checkpoint timings, and the timestamp comparison does
not isolate reflection from the changed representation.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/003fd04d-7d4e-4f55-9a77-584d353c93ab)
retains all raw samples and benchstat output. All 22 benchmark actions and
benchstat passed. The parent failed afterward because cleanup named two
source files deleted by the candidate; the source tree was already clean.
The measurements were preserved and not rerun.

OK. So a real cost, but what's not answered yet is how much this is amortized on a real-world application checkpoint.

However, given that we already have something that works, that this would be a regression, and that building on this mechanism (which IIUC you are planning to do), perhaps it's worth looking at whether this can be solved without this overhead? Perhaps via code generation like the rest of the stateify package, perhaps with a generic function with a type switch (which IIRC will inline correctly on each type-specific invocation to effectively remove the `switch` so long as the types are distinguishable, we use this trick in https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/5dd59c99442c6692227bdff0e1f8f973d96ade07/pkg/bpf/input_bytes.go#L51 for example).
Yeah, I'm pushing to optimize this a bit.
If it finds other stateify runtime optimizations, all the better btw. Every millisecond counts in that path.

Updated in [bfeafd451](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/bfeafd451).
Type names, fields and codec dispatch are now cached at registration;
Save/Load no longer constructs an adapter for each binary-coded value.

The follow-up `benchstat` comparison uses the same timestamp-bearing
`tcpip.ReceivableControlMessages` value for all three implementations:

```text
Measure               Original hooks   Initial codec   Revised
Save (us/call)                  8.066           9.351     6.881
Load (us/call)                 10.164          10.991     8.813
Save (allocs/call)                 80              94        68
Load (allocs/call)                138             151       125
Encoded bytes                    494             521       521
```

Relative to the original conversion hooks, Save is 14.70% faster and
Load is 13.29% faster (both p<0.001, n=12). Compared with the initial
codec implementation, they are 26.41% and 19.81% faster. The 27-byte
encoding increase remains.

The ordinary map-decoding control measured 324.9 ns/op versus 331.5 for
the original implementation (no significant difference, p=.682). It was
2.49% slower than the initial codec implementation (317.0 ns/op,
p=.008). An [earlier comparison](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/d67982e1-db7e-40c6-a307-52e95aa38215)
measured a 5.88% slowdown against that implementation; its cause remains
unestablished.

The [run](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/91d7662c-227f-4afd-bdc2-e465c4f117e2)
used one Linux AMD64 worker, precompiled binaries, fixed CPU affinity,
and twelve balanced three-version blocks. The measured sources were
[original hooks](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/6500a6c00),
[initial codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/b27217132), and
[revised codec](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a8081ccb5); the
amendment preserves that implementation after rebasing. These are
focused
serialization measurements, not complete-checkpoint or application
throughput results.

Assisted-by: Codex

Updated the codec dispatch to use type switches while preserving
Register(Type). Explicit state methods take precedence, Type-only empty
structs retain their existing behavior, and binary codecs handle the
remaining registered foreign structs. Names and fields still come from
the existing type databases.

The comparison used the original hooks, the previous cached-flag codec,
and this switch on one worker, with 12 balanced blocks of the same
pointer/map/slice and ReceivableControlMessages benchmarks. Compilation
completed before measurement, with no fresh compilation during samples.
All versions use the same benchmark bodies; original to switch includes
the full codec change.

```text
                         Original    Cached flag    Type switch
Timestamp save (us/op)      9.5225       8.4035         8.2445
Timestamp load (us/op)     12.2540      10.6320        10.5390
Save allocations/op           80           68             68
Load allocations/op          138          125            125
Encoded bytes                 494          521            521
```

The switch showed no statistically significant timing difference from
the cached-flag version across all eight benchmarks. Timestamp save and
load each used 96 fewer bytes per operation, with unchanged allocation
counts. Compared with the original hooks, timestamp save was 13.42%
faster and load was 14.00% faster in this sample (p < .001); none of the
six ordinary benchmarks showed a significant timing difference.

These are focused state-codec measurements, not whole-checkpoint results
or proof of equivalent performance. The larger binary time format also
preserves zero values and numeric zone offsets. This version and these
measurements do not include BinaryAppender.

Measured sources and result:

Original hooks: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/6500a6c00
Cached flag: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/a8081ccb5
Type switch: https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/dc3635f89
https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/eacaac2c-8de9-46c6-b98b-d2b0477a973a

The last comment captures the BinaryAppender benchmark results; it reduced allocations but didn't improve speed

@EtiennePerot @nybidari the reviewed [netip migration][1] is ready.
It replaces the core TCP/IP address, subnet and address/port types with
netip equivalents. It needs this PR's support for saving and restoring
foreign types, so #15476 must land before I can submit it as an

Can you benchmark this?

I'm not too worried but gVisor save/restore is very time-sensitive and CPU-bound so I'm wondering what the extra time paid to reflection costs.
Looks good but curious to see updated benchmarks with BinaryAppender to see if that actually improves things.

Would it make sense to use the `encoding.BinaryAppender` interface instead here? This would allow the `saveBinary` function below to allocate a hopefully-large-enough slice and reuse it across multiple instances of the same type, or use some `sync.Pool` for them created at stateify begin time and cleared afterwards. For predictably-sized objects, we could also have an optional "optimal preallocated slice size" that could be specified during type registration, so that the correct size is consistently allocated.

source.title: Allow libc thread creation in cgo filters
source.body:
Allow libc thread creation in cgo filters

The cgo seccomp policies allowed clone3, but their legacy clone rule
only accepted the Go runtime's thread arguments. The musl pthread_create
used by the static plugin runtime calls legacy clone with parent-settid
and child-cleartid flags and nonzero TID pointers, so that call was
denied.

Permit musl's exact thread flags in the Sentry and gofer cgo policies.
Keep the Go rule and require cgo for the additional libc rule. Exercise
the generated filters with both thread forms and reject process,
namespace and exit-signal variants in non-instrumented builds.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit
source.body:
Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit

Updating oom_score_adj for an exited, unreaped process could fail for a
nonroot caller: Linux makes the process's proc files root-owned after
exit [1], so opening the file failed with EACCES. The no-op-on-exit
handling added in 88f736992 covered ENOENT and ESRCH but missed this case.

Share the existing pidfd liveness check with the OOM-score helper and
ignore EACCES only after confirming that the process has exited. Preserve
the original error when the process is alive or its state is unknown.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/fs/proc/base.c#L1848-L1869

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Restore original cgroup membership in tests
source.body:
Restore original cgroup membership in tests

Cgroup2Test moved the test process back to the mounted cgroup root after
migration instead of the group it started in. This discarded its original
membership. In a delegated cgroup namespace, the move could also fail with
EBUSY when the namespace root had enabled controllers, leaving test groups
occupied.

Save the original v2 membership before changing groups or controllers and
restore it during scope cleanup and fixture teardown. Report restoration
errors instead of ignoring them.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Validate netfilter query sizes and permissions
source.body:
Validate netfilter query sizes and permissions

67fcf4020 fixed the missing-table error that had stopped Syzkaller [1],
but request validation still differed from Linux. GET_INFO accepted
oversized buffers and checked their length before permissions, while
GET_ENTRIES looked up the table before checking the declared entry size.

Require exact request sizes before table lookup and check GET_INFO
permissions first, matching Linux's IPv4 and IPv6 paths [2][3]. Extend the
existing IPv4 missing-table regressions and cover the same size and
permission precedence for IPv6.

[1]: https://buildkite.com/gvisor/pipeline/builds/49879#01a114dd-05ce-42c1-8321-2df04d84e781
[2]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/69f80fef3/net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c
[3]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/69f80fef3/net/ipv6/netfilter/ip6_tables.c

source.title: Drop privilege in the Landlock rejection test
source.body:
Drop privilege in the Landlock rejection test

RestrictSelfWithoutNoNewPrivsFails expected EPERM even when the caller
had CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Linux allows that capability to authorize restriction
without no_new_privs [1]. The test lacked this precondition under its
privileged native fixture.

Drop effective CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the existing child and check that
no_new_privs is unset before exercising the rejection path.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/e5f0a698b/security/landlock/syscalls.c#L491-L497

source.title: Preserve XML test suites during collation
source.body:
Preserve XML test suites during collation

The per-case report collation introduced by d54df9b21 extracted test
cases by searching for XML delimiters. A report containing several
self-closing cases retained only its first case; self-closing cases
after the last explicit closing tag were also lost. Such reports can
come from the discovery fallback that runs the entire test binary.

Parse and combine complete test suites, preserving their attributes,
case contents and properties. Sum the report counts and durations and
retain the earliest timestamp. Parse all inputs before replacing the
output so malformed reports cannot silently produce partial results.

Keep the private collator separately testable with actual input and
output files, including mixed failure, skip and self-closing cases.
Include the runner tests in the existing unit CI selection.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Bind SYN cookies to the client sequence number
source.body:
Bind SYN cookies to the client sequence number

A duplicate ACK could recreate an accepted socket after the original
connection closed. SYN cookies added the client's sequence number
outside the hash, so the advances caused by both FINs canceled during
validation. The server then accepted a socket whose peer had already
finished closing.

Hash the client's initial sequence number instead. Preserve the cookie's
MSS and expiration encoding, and exercise duplicate closing ACKs both
queued behind the first ACK and delivered after the endpoint closes.

prs.head: 68347953351371f33907fdf0a19b783d61671364

items.body: i am not familiar enough with changes at PR, probably @nybidari can take a look

## Code Review

This pull request updates the TCP CUBIC congestion control implementation to comply with RFC 9438. Key changes include tracking the window at the start of an epoch with cwndEpoch, updating the Reno-friendly window estimate calculation based on received ACKs, and introducing HandleWindowRestart to manage idle periods. Additionally, comprehensive unit tests have been added to validate these updates. The reviewer suggested optimizing the cubicCwnd calculation by replacing math.Pow(t, 3.0) with direct multiplication t * t * t to improve performance on hot paths.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Using math.Pow(t, 3.0) is significantly slower than direct multiplication t * t * t because math.Pow handles arbitrary real exponents and has substantial function call and computational overhead. Since cubicCwnd is evaluated on every ACK in congestion avoidance, optimizing this to t * t * t provides a noticeable performance improvement.

```suggestion
return c.C*t*t*t + max(c.WMax, c.cwndEpoch)
```
citation needed. did you benchmark it?

I got curious so I did, gemini-code-assist is correct.

```
                   │   pow.txt    │               mul.txt               │
                   │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base                │
     X-20            13.670n ± 5%   1.912n ± 2%  -86.01% (p=0.000 n=20)
     CubicCwndX-20   12.625n ± 2%   1.934n ± 2%  -84.68% (p=0.000 n=20)

```

Replaced `math.Pow(t, 3)` with `t*t*t`, keeping multiplication by `C`
after the cube. Thanks for benchmarking it. The existing tests pass on
AMD64 and ARM64.

items.body:
Rebased onto master at [3f35bca89]. This rebase leaves the topic
changes unchanged.

@nybidari, please take another look at the [rebased head].

[3f35bca89]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/3f35bca89c44d2b03f6b2fcc4510b05bd1397828
[rebased head]: https://github.com/google/gvisor/commit/776b86bce2baa17457cb9375e8a15f8b437d5737

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

## Code Review

This pull request initializes the EndSequence field in the rackControl struct and introduces a new test, TestRACKInitialDeliverySequence, to ensure correct behavior with initial sequence numbers. The reviewer identified an additional issue where RTTSeq should also be initialized to the initial sequence number (iss) to prevent incorrect sequence comparisons when the ISN is in the upper half of the sequence space, and provided a code suggestion to address this.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Similar to `EndSequence` and `FACK`, `RTTSeq` is a sequence number field (`seqnum.Value`) in `rackControl` used for sequence comparisons (specifically in `updateRACKReorderWindow` to filter DSACKs once per round trip). If `RTTSeq` is left uninitialized (defaulting to `0`), and the connection's ISN is in the upper half of the sequence number space (i.e., `iss > 2^31`), the comparison `snd.SndUna.LessThan(rc.RTTSeq)` (which evaluates `(iss + 1).LessThan(0)`) will incorrectly evaluate to `true` on the very first ACK. This causes any DSACK received on the first ACK to be prematurely ignored. Initializing `rc.RTTSeq` to `iss` prevents this sequence comparison bug.

```suggestion
rc.EndSequence = iss
	rc.RTTSeq = iss
```

Thanks, confirmed. RTTSeq now starts at the connection ISN too. The
regression covers the first DSACK expansion, suppression within the same
round, and expansion after the round boundary for low, high and wrapping
ISNs. The original high/wrap cases fail; the corrected TCP/RACK suites on
both CPUs, focused race coverage and owning analyzers pass.

source.title: Initialize RACK sequence markers from the ISN
source.body:
Initialize RACK sequence markers from the ISN

Manual-clock TCP tests can transmit at monotonic time zero, tying RACK's
unset timestamp. Comparing packet sequences with a zero delivery marker
could then report loss before any delivery.

The initial DSACK round boundary also used zero. For high initial
sequence numbers, this suppressed reordering-window growth regardless of
the clock origin.

Initialize both markers relative to the connection's ISN. Cover initial
delivery ordering and DSACK expansion once per round with low,
high-half, and wrapping sequence numbers.

items.body:
Instead of adding this method, can we defer releasing the view to handle the leak in error cases. Something like:

```
view := pkt.ToView()
ok := false
defer func() {
	if !ok {
		view.Release()
	}
}()
....
checker.IPv4(c.t, view, checker.SrcAddr(StackAddr), checker.DstAddr(TestAddr))
ok = true
return view
```

I replaced the new AsView API with the existing ToView and cleanup.Make.
Each reader defers Clean immediately after obtaining the view, then calls
Release when returning ownership to the caller. This covers Fatal/Goexit
without a conditional cleanup flag. CheckNoPacketTimeout still releases
an unexpected packet before aborting.

The cleanup, TCP, dual-stack and context analyzer checks pass. A temporary
probe also reproduced the old leaks and confirmed cleanup through all
four real abort paths. The probe is not part of the change.

source.title: Wait for TCP receive timestamp readiness
source.body:
Wait for TCP receive timestamp readiness

Linux can return from SO_TIMESTAMP before receive timestamping becomes
active. TcpSCMPriority sent its checked data immediately and could
receive only TCP_INQ, failing the control-message ordering assertions.
Linux's timestamp selftest also waits for activation [1].

Exchange one-byte probes on the existing native TCP connection until a
receive timestamp arrives, retaining the enabled socket for the ordering
check. Bound readiness by one monotonic deadline and report the count of
untimestamped probes. The original ancillary-message assertions remain
the behavior under test.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/ce6f6cffa

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Avoid late checkpoint waits in tests
source.body:
Avoid late checkpoint waits in tests

TestCheckpointRestoreAnnotation started its workload before issuing
WaitCheckpoint. That API waits for the next generation after the RPC
arrives, so a fast checkpoint could finish first and leave the test
waiting for another checkpoint that the workload never requested.

Wait for the existing proc-fd response instead. The workload opens that
file before triggering its checkpoint, so the response remains tied to
the intended generation. Remove the same registration assumption from
two other test paths: their synchronous Checkpoint call already reports
completion and errors, and starting a waiter goroutine did not establish
that the server had registered it.

Keep the next-generation API used by runsc wait --checkpoint. Exercise
that contract directly with an already completed generation and the next
generation's error, using synctest to wait for registration.

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Consolidate GPU driver preparation
source.body:
Consolidate GPU driver preparation

Installation and checksum commands used separate download and hashing
paths. Share one transfer that copies every byte, including final data
returned with EOF, and rejects failed transfers. Recognize absent
NVIDIA .run installers by HTTP status and continue validating the other
architecture after an expected missing installer.

Resolve the host checksum when selecting the requested driver. Before
removing an existing driver, require a successful host inspection and
PCI preflight, then download, verify and close the replacement
executable. Propagate the operation context through host commands and
distinguish a missing nvidia-smi from a failed installed-driver query.

Use the same host eligibility selection for installation and listing,
and replace complete output files so a shorter list cannot leave stale
data.

items.body: r? @nybidari

Really impressive and long-overdue cleanup, @tamird! Replacing `tcpip.Address`, `tcpip.Subnet`, and transport address/port pairs with standard library `net/netip` types removes a huge amount of custom prefix logic and allocation churn across the stack.

Given the scale of this change (166 files, ~9k lines diff), would you be open to breaking this up into a few smaller, stacked PRs? That would make review, bisection, and merging much smoother:

1. **`pkg/state` serialization support:** Registering `netip.Addr`, `netip.Prefix`, and `netip.AddrPort` via `registerBinary` and the tests in `pkg/state/tests/netip_test.go` can land as a standalone, zero-risk PR first.
2. **Pre-refactoring test cleanups:** The IPv6 control-message fixture bugfix (19-byte literal) and converting non-contiguous masks to CIDR in `stack_test.go` can also land independently ahead of time.
3. **Core Netstack Migration:** The remaining type alias switch and caller updates in `pkg/tcpip` and sentry.

> Given the scale of this change (166 files, ~9k lines diff), would you be open to breaking this up into a few smaller, stacked PRs? That would make review, bisection, and merging much smoother:

Certainly, happy to break it up.

> 1. **`pkg/state` serialization support:** Registering `netip.Addr`, `netip.Prefix`, and `netip.AddrPort` via `registerBinary` and the tests in `pkg/state/tests/netip_test.go` can land as a standalone, zero-risk PR first.

That's true, but kind of pointless because that code would also be inert until (3) lands. So I'd rather not do this artificial split.

> 2. **Pre-refactoring test cleanups:** The IPv6 control-message fixture bugfix (19-byte literal) and converting non-contiguous masks to CIDR in `stack_test.go` can also land independently ahead of time.

Makes sense, I'll do this.

> 3. **Core Netstack Migration:** The remaining type alias switch and caller updates in `pkg/tcpip` and sentry.

I think this will reduce the diff by less than 100 loc, fwiw.

I'll address the other comments of course. I'm on EU time right now, so these updates will come tomorrow.

Prefactoring landed:
- https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15770
- https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15771

This is ready for another look please!

Addressed invalid-address handling in both locations.

Assisted-by: Codex

Indexing `addrBytes[i]` or `maskBytes[i]` inside the loop can panic out-of-bounds if `filterAddr` has a different address family or length than `addr`/`mask`, or if an invalid `netip.Addr{}` is provided (where `AsSlice()` returns nil).

Consider guarding lengths up front:
```go
if len(addrBytes) == 0 || len(addrBytes) != len(maskBytes) || len(addrBytes) != len(filterBytes) {
	return false != invert
}
```

Added the length checks before indexing, with an explicit case for an omitted IPHeaderFilter so existing wildcard rules still match. The regression covers invalid addresses, mismatched families and wildcard filters.
Changed this to `addr.IsValid() && !addr.IsUnspecified()`, so the zero value is correctly treated as unspecified.

prs.title: pkg/state: Verify registered types in `race` builds only.
prs.head: 344906981e5d3bdb70d4e6366e5d261adcf6c510

items.body:
Restoring cheap registration makes sense: startup should not pay for field
metadata that is only needed by save/restore. The inline comments cover a
repeatability bug in the new test and the split ownership of registration.

Could the title and description describe this as deferring ordinary type
metadata work until save/restore in non-race builds? Validation still runs
there, and binary registrations still validate eagerly, so "Verify
registered types in race builds only" does not describe the full behavior.
Please also include the command and before/after startup measurements
behind the 0.3 ms improvement so the result is reproducible.

This is a source review; I have not run the repeated-test case.

Assisted-by: Codex

This assertion fails when the test is repeated in one process with
`-test.count=2`. The Save/Load calls below increment
`lazyTypeFieldsCalls`, and nothing resets it, so the second run attributes
the previous run's metadata lookups to `Register`.

Please compare the counter immediately before and after registration, or
otherwise isolate the observation. More generally, could this regression
focus on registration not calling `StateFields`? The direct assertions
about both global maps couple it to the storage implementation, while the
generic round-trip overlaps existing state tests.

This introduces a second place that publishes entries into
`globalTypeDatabase`: non-race ordinary registration writes here, while
race-enabled and binary registration go through `register`. The policy
also has to be reconstructed from `raceEnabled` checks in `Register`,
`register`, and `lookupTypeInfo`.

Could we give name-to-type registration one owner and separate it from
metadata collection/validation? That would make the eager versus deferred
work explicit without duplicating the map update. The cheap path should
still avoid `StateFields` and reverse-map construction; binary types still
need their explicit metadata because they do not implement `Type`.

The race-only integrity checks are useful. The concern is spreading their
policy across the registration and lookup paths, not removing them.

source.title: tcp: reject ambiguous loss-probe RTT samples
source.body:
tcp: reject ambiguous loss-probe RTT samples

Tail loss probes bypassed resendSegment's RTT measurement invalidation. A
probe retransmitting the measured sequence reset its measurement time,
so a later ambiguous ACK changed SRTT and RTO using time since the probe.

Move the existing invalidation to sendSegment's retransmission branch so
all data retransmission paths apply Karn's rule (RFC 6298, section 3).
Timestamp-based ACK measurements remain independently eligible. Add a
packet regression covering the ambiguous ACK, echoes of either timestamp,
and resumed measurement when new data is acknowledged.

Assisted-by: Codex

Accept architecture-independent KCOV records

The KCOV test assumes every reported PC lies in the top 2 GiB of the
address space. gVisor encodes package, function and block identifiers
instead of instruction addresses, and Linux's address layout also varies
by architecture and configuration.

Check that coverage records are nonzero and fit within the mapped buffer.
Remove the unused constant that still describes the old 32-bit encoding.
The existing test fails before this change and passes afterward in both
instrumented AMD64 gVisor configurations.

source.title: Wait for native TCP timestamp activation
source.body:
Wait for native TCP timestamp activation

TcpSCMPriority expected a timestamp on the first packet after enabling
SO_TIMESTAMP. With CONFIG_JUMP_LABEL, Linux schedules netstamp_work to
activate packet timestamping asynchronously [1], so that packet could
arrive with only TCP_INQ.

Send and consume fresh payloads until native timestamping is ready,
using the existing timeout as a monotonic readiness bound. Retry only a
valid sole TCP_INQ record. Keep timestamp-before-INQ ordering, record
lengths, queue values and absence of extra records strict on every
response; malformed or reordered metadata fails immediately. Preserve
gVisor's existing optional timestamp behavior.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/fd73f4a66/net/core/dev.c#L2395-L2424

Assisted-by: Codex

prs.title: Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs
prs.head: b143d86cb32a1eaa516324f52423b395a0123126

items.body:
Thanks for this PR! 

Linux uses Minshall's variant of Nagle where a partial segment:
- is sent if all the outstanding segments (unacked) are full sized segments.
- waits if there is atleast one small sized segment which is unacknowledged. 

My understanding is the change here waits for an ACK for both cases while sending a partial segment. That check isn't new, but now applies it to the tail of a split write. Previously the remaining partial packet copied the previous packet's flags which was sent and skipped Nagle. My concern is for the loopback cases with no offload or GSO and we enable nagle by default in runsc. Even with GSO, it still waits when only full-sized segments are in flight, where Linux would send it. 

Can you please add a test for an idle connection without GSO and verify whether the partial segment goes out without waiting for an ACK?

If it waits, I think the fix would be something like tracking the end of the last sent partial segment and holding only while it's unacknowledged (similar to linux).

> Can you please add a test for an idle connection without GSO

Regarding [Nayana's request](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15926#issuecomment-6295602307):

The earlier change incorrectly treated all unacknowledged data as a
reason to hold a partial segment. Linux's Minshall variant waits only
when an earlier partial segment is still unacknowledged.

The amendment records that segment's end sequence number, including a
partial GSO tail. An idle MSS-plus-tail write now sends the tail without
waiting for the full segment's ACK. Later small writes wait until the
partial segment is fully acknowledged; full-sized sends and
retransmissions do not replace that marker. TCP_CORK keeps its separate
hold.

The new regression covers idle and full-only outstanding prefixes, with
and without GSO, then partial and exact-end ACKs. All four cases
reproduce the old failure and pass with the fix. Both complete TCP
suites and the owning analyzers pass, as does canonical BUILD lint.

Assisted-by: OpenAI Codex, acting on behalf of Tamir Duberstein.

Nice! 

LGTM.

@nybidari reminder to mark this for import!

EDIT: ah it's already marked
Please rebase.

> Please rebase.

@nybidari will do but why?
Internal presubmits were failing, all good now.
nit: this can just be `if seg.payloadSize()%s.MaxPayloadSize != 0 {` retransmissions never get here.

Removed the extra guard. The `SndNxt` bound already excludes
retransmissions. This also fixes fresh data released by the CORK timer:
that path assigns flags before sending, so it did not satisfy `newData`
and its partial tail was not recorded.

I added CORK expiry to the existing regression in both GSO modes. Both
cases fail before the change and pass afterward; the existing Nagle/CORK
controls, owning analyzers and buildifier also pass.

[Validation](https://app.buildbuddy.io/invocation/bcc23e70-b81b-4c66-a83c-8fb7a7cb0aea)

source.title: Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs
source.body:
Send full TCP segments without waiting for ACKs

With segmentation offload enabled, TCP's send budget can cover several
segments. Nagle compared queued data with that entire budget and could
hold full-sized writes until a probe timer fired.

Use the MSS to decide whether Nagle or TCP_CORK has enough data to send.
Send the full-segment prefix while retaining a partial tail for later
coalescing. Leave that tail unassigned until it can be sent, so a window
update cannot bypass the same decision. Preserve the existing exceptions
for short windows and writes that cannot be combined. Nagle permits full
segments while earlier data remains unacknowledged [1].

Exercise full writes and held tails with and without offload, using a
stopped clock so retransmission timers cannot hide a stalled write.
Complete requested checksum offload in the channel fixture so packet
checks can validate aggregate GSO output.

[1]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html#section-3.7.4

Assisted-by: Codex

source.title: Ignore OOM score permission errors after exit
source.body:
Updating oom_score_adj for an exited, unreaped process could fail for a
nonroot caller: Linux makes the process's proc files root-owned after
exit [1], so opening the file failed with EACCES. The no-op-on-exit
handling added in 88f736992 covered ENOENT and ESRCH but missed this case.

Share the existing pidfd liveness check with the OOM-score helper and
ignore EACCES only after confirming that the process has exited. Preserve
the original error when the process is alive or its state is unknown.

[1]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/830b3c68c/fs/proc/base.c#L1848-L1869

source.title: Report the host's ephemeral port range in hostinet
source.body:
Report the host's ephemeral port range in hostinet

Host-networked applications read a fixed ephemeral port range from
procfs, even when their sockets use a different range in the host network
namespace. Read the host value during initialization and refresh it from
the destination host on restore.

Run the existing port-exhaustion tests in a private network namespace
with a small range. Hostinet cannot change that sysctl from inside the
sandbox; without this setup, the tests skip rather than exhaust the
host's much larger range. Extend the existing restore test to check the
destination range.

source.title: Restore tracereplay tests to routine CI
source.body:
Restore tracereplay tests to routine CI

TestBasic used its absolute temporary directory in the Unix-domain socket
address. Bazel's TEST_TMPDIR can make that address exceed sockaddr_un's
limit, failing bind before any trace replay as reported in #10045.

Resolve the input file before entering a test-owned temporary directory,
then use a relative socket pathname. Keep the directory's absolute path
long to cover this failure and let testing clean up the fixture.

Remove the tracereplay unit-test exclusion.

source.title: Retain output when runtime test discovery fails
source.body:
Retain output when runtime test discovery fails

When Java test discovery failed, the runner reported only exit status 1.
The launcher had printed `No java executable at java` to stdout, but the
Java proctor and outer Docker execution error discarded their captured
output. Retain that output in both errors and preserve the underlying
errors with wrapping.

The exact changes exposed the launcher diagnostic in a remote gVisor
run. With these two error-return lines unchanged, a later run with the
corrected recipe passed discovery and both focused runtime owners.
This two-line change has no Java image dependency. The standalone
upstream checkout has not been executed. Full Java discovery completed
in both modes; its separate runtime failures remain under diagnosis.

Prepared with Codex assistance.

strconv error cause with the failing field and mapping. Cover syntax
and range errors for each field, high unsigned values, and multiple
mappings.

prs.title: filecache: reuse the concurrent scan fixture
prs.head: dd1bbf30e4f345371b487ecec00361f99a95f907

items.body: I also checked the two findings outside the diff. Both are in the existing production code: a missing file can stop the scan for that group, and Close does not wait for the startup scan. I left those out of this test-only PR. The test waits for scanning to finish before closing each cache. Those production issues need separate fixes and tests.

Reworks the filecache concurrent-scan test so it builds one fixture in the current layout and reuses it across trials. The test now covers the in-place scan's "already in the LRU, so don't evict" check instead of the legacy migration branch. No blocking bugs were found.

### Additional findings (lines outside the diff)
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/filecache/filecache.go:521` — Pre-existing, not introduced by this PR: if a file disappears while the scan is running, the scan stops for the rest of that group.
- Sequence: `AddFile(k)` runs before the scan reaches `k`, then `DeleteFile(k)` or a size eviction unlinks the file. When the scan reaches `k`, `os.Stat` returns `NotFound`.
- Only `InvalidArgument` is tolerated (line 514), so `WalkDir` aborts.
- Every remaining file in that group stays on disk but never enters the LRU, so it is never evicted. #7924 removed the earlier `NotFound` tolerance.

The reworked test does one `AddFile` per trial, so it can't hit this.
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/filecache/filecache.go:270` — Pre-existing, not introduced by this PR: `Close` doesn't wait for the scan, because the scan starts with a bare `go c.scanDir()` instead of `c.wg.Go`. That is why the test's deferred cleanup at `filecache_test.go:689` has to call `WaitForDirectoryScanToComplete()` itself. In production, a scan or migration that is still running can write after `Close` has synced and removed `boot_id`.

**[Re-run review](https://app.buildbuddy.io/workflows/run?action_name=Code+review&branch=sluongng%2Ffilecache-scan-fixture&env_preset=AGENT_REVIEW&repo_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fbuildbuddy-io%2Fbuildbuddy)**

<sub>Reviewed with [`bb agent review`](https://www.buildbuddy.io/docs/cli-commands#bb-agent-review) on BuildBuddy Workflows</sub>

No test now runs the legacy migration at the same time as `AddFile`. The old fixture was the only one that did, through the migration branch at `filecache.go:778-797` (`Remove(k)`, link the legacy path, unlink it). `TestFileCacheEvictionAfterSubdirPrefixing` and `TestFileCacheEvictionAfterStartupScan` both call `WaitForDirectoryScanToComplete()` before `AddFile`. So "leaving legacy migration coverage in its existing tests" covers migration alone, not migration during a concurrent add. Upgraded executors still on the flat layout run exactly that path at startup. Consider keeping a legacy fixture with a small trial count (for example, 5–10), or adding a separate small test for it.

Good catch. I kept 100 current-layout trials and added five old-layout migration trials. Each migration trial gets a fresh cache directory and adds a file while the startup scan runs. All 100 files are still checked in every trial.

The re-added file is a weaker check than before:
- `sourcePaths[i]` is the same inode that is already in the cache. `ANON` uses `Clone`, which uses `FastCopy`, which is `os.Link` on Linux.
- If the scan hasn't reached `k` yet, `l.Remove(k)` does nothing and `cloneOrLink` treats `EEXIST` as success (`FastCopy` in `fastcopy_linux.go`). The re-add is then a complete no-op.
- The old test re-added a separate `action.output` file, and neither version checks file contents.

Writing a fresh copy each trial is cheap: one file, compared with the 100 the old version wrote.

Fixed. Each trial now writes a fresh source file before starting the cache, then re-adds that file. It no longer reuses the inode already in the cache. The test also checks the contents of the linked re-added file.

This may not fix the Windows timeout. Each trial still links 100 files with `FastLinkFile`, which is a `CopyFileW` on Windows. The next `NewFileCache` then deletes all 100 with `os.RemoveAll(TempDir())`, for about 10k copies and 10k deletes in total. The change removes about 100 writes and 100 migration copy-and-unlink operations per trial, roughly half the I/O. As the description says, Windows CI needs to confirm this fits the `size = "small"` budget.

Agreed. The first revision passed the Windows executor CI job with the existing budget. That is one passing run, not proof that the flake is gone. The updated test keeps all link checks and needs a new Windows CI result. I have not changed any timeout or wait budget.

Nit: `for i := range n` (line 702) shadows the re-added `i` from line 695 (this predates the PR). Also, every trial now shares one `filecacheRoot`, so the failure message should say which node was re-added. Renaming the outer variable (for example, to `readded`) and including it in the message fixes both.
Fixed. The variable is now named `readded`, and link failures include both the trial number and the re-added node.

Low confidence: nothing forces `AddFile` to overlap the scan, and that was true before too. The in-place scan no longer copies files while holding the lock, so it is much shorter. More trials may now run entirely before or after the scan and never exercise the race, and the test can't report how many trials actually overlapped.

Agreed: overlap still depends on timing. I made that clear in the test and PR description and kept a few migration trials. The existing test API has no way to pause the scan at the relevant point. I left a new scan hook out of this test-only fix rather than adding sleeps or claiming that overlap is guaranteed.

source.title: Enable vhost-net in x86 guest kernels
source.body:
The x86 guest configs disabled vhost-net, so the guest could not provide `/dev/vhost-net` to nested userspace network backends (#13604). This enables `CONFIG_VHOST_NET`, plus the `CONFIG_VHOST` and `CONFIG_VHOST_IOTLB` options it selects, in the 5.15 and 6.18 configs, and rebuilds both kernels.

This supersedes #13803, which targeted the 6.1 config that #13812 replaced with 6.18.

Rebuilding 5.15 changes the default guest kernel digest, so existing x86_64 VM snapshots are invalidated on the next executor rollout.

prs.title: Enable vhost-net in x86 guest kernels
prs.head: 1c8ea1521a8b39fb5e39346367c605ea51706f4b

items.body:
Turns on `CONFIG_VHOST_NET` (along with `CONFIG_VHOST` and `CONFIG_VHOST_IOTLB`) in the x86_64 5.15 and 6.18 guest kernel configs, and updates `deps.bzl` to point at the rebuilt kernel binaries.

### Additional findings (lines outside the diff)
- `enterprise/server/cmd/goinit/main.go:241` — `/dev/vhost-net` stays root-only (0600). goinit relaxes `/dev/net/tun` and `/dev/fuse` to 0666 because the guest has no udev. On a normal distro, udev also makes `/dev/vhost-net` 0666, but it isn't added to this list. As a result, rootless Podman/QEMU, or any action running as a non-root user, gets EACCES when opening it, and only root in the guest benefits from this change. Consider adding `/dev/vhost-net` here.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/BUILD:10` — The default 5.15 kernel is built from the bare `v5.15` tag (5.15.0). This target has no `git_tag`, so the build uses tag `v5.15`. This PR now compiles the vhost/vhost_net driver into every x86_64 guest without the later 5.15.y fixes, such as the iotlb hung-thread fix and the vhost_net ubuf refcount fix. `rebuild.sh:48` already recommends pinning a point release, as the 6.18 target does with `v6.18.57`.
- `enterprise/server/remote_execution/containers/firecracker/firecracker_test.go:418` — No test checks that `/dev/vhost-net` exists. `TestFirecrackerRunSimple` already runs `stat` on `/dev/fuse` and `/dev/net/tun`. Adding `/dev/vhost-net` to the amd64 branch would catch a kernel uploaded from the wrong config, or a later config edit that drops VHOST_NET. The new sha256 values in `deps.bzl` only show the file matches what was uploaded, not which config it was built from.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/microvm-kernel-aarch64-v5.10.config:2135` — arm64 is still `# CONFIG_VHOST_NET is not set`, with no TODO, so the fix for #13604 only covers x86_64. TUN is already tracked with a TODO in the test; this should be tracked the same way.
- `enterprise/vmsupport/kernel/rebuild.sh:83` — The build can't be reproduced to check the new hashes. `KBUILD_BUILD_TIMESTAMP`, `KBUILD_BUILD_USER` and `KBUILD_BUILD_HOST` are never pinned, so a reviewer can't rebuild and confirm that `10b243f5…` and `4c27704a…` came from these configs. This problem predates the PR, but it matters most when a PR's whole change is a new hash.

**[Re-run review](https://app.buildbuddy.io/workflows/run?action_name=Code+review&branch=guest-kernel-vhost-net&env_preset=AGENT_REVIEW&repo_url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fbuildbuddy-io%2Fbuildbuddy)**

<sub>Reviewed with [`bb agent review`](https://www.buildbuddy.io/docs/cli-commands#bb-agent-review) on BuildBuddy Workflows</sub>

This config is missing `CONFIG_VHOST_TASK=y`. In kernels 6.4 and later, enabling `VHOST` automatically turns on `VHOST_TASK` too. `rebuild.sh:75` runs `make olddefconfig`, so the kernel that was actually built has it, but the checked-in file doesn't. The new header line also says VHOST_NET only pulls in VHOST and VHOST_IOTLB, which is wrong for 6.18. If someone compares this file with the guest's `/proc/config.gz`, they'll see a difference that shouldn't be there.

This will invalidate every x86_64 VM snapshot. The 5.15 kernel digest is part of every x86_64 snapshot key, so on rollout all recycled runners and CI workflows will cold-boot. Any kernel change has that cost, but it's worth deciding on purpose. Options are shipping in 6.18 only for now, or bundling this with the next 5.15 rebuild that's needed anyway.

Heads-up: vhost worker threads behave differently on 6.18 than on 5.15. `CONFIG_VHOST_ENABLE_FORK_OWNER_CONTROL` is unset, and that now matters because VHOST is built in. On 6.18 the worker threads always run in the owner's thread group and count against its pids/`RLIMIT_NPROC` limits; on 5.15 they're separate kernel threads. Mostly relevant for anyone comparing the two kernels in the upgrade experiment.

prs.title: Select Firecracker guest kernel versions
prs.head: 8c704d5324518b02f430a3f5f0f9388549c65eab

items.body:
The context is in the referenced ticket: we want the kernel version to be an explicit property of the execution environment because gvisor's test suite tests the behavior of the host kernel in order to compare it to gvisor's behavior.

Without an execution property we get incorrect test result caching.

@tamird got it, thanks for clarifying. I agree that for tests that explicitly exercise kernel behavior, changing the guest kernel without changing the action cache key is a correctness problem. We'll need to discuss this internally and reach consensus on what kernel-selection API and support policy we can commit to, including how we handle updates and retire older versions. I understand why an explicit execution property would be useful here; we need to work through those support implications before committing to it.
@bduffany makes sense, thanks!

Currently we can switch kernel versions without breaking people (we have a process for ramping this up via experiment, carefully monitoring errors, and working w/ people to address breakages), but this property would lock it in as a public API that we have to support, which I'm not sure we can commit to right now.

If you give a bit more context for why you need to opt in to 5.15, I think we could consider some alternatives here. FWIW, v5.15 is EOL in December of this year
